content.text:
5: Building Materials and Embodied Carbon

Beyond operational emissions, the "embodied carbon" of building materials contributes significantly to the sector's overall footprint. Embodied carbon refers to the sum of all greenhouse gas emissions released during the lifecycle of materials, including extraction, manufacturing, transport, construction, and disposal. It accounts for an estimated 11% of annual global climate-warming GHG emissions. As buildings become more operationally efficient, the share of embodied carbon in their total lifecycle emissions is expected to grow.

The holistic approach to building decarbonization recognizes that addressing climate goals in the built environment requires considering both operational and embodied emissions throughout a building's lifecycle. While improving operational energy efficiency 💬️ (heating, cooling, lighting) has been a long-standing focus, the substantial contribution of embodied carbon, the emissions associated with materials from extraction to disposal, is gaining increasing recognition. For instance, cement production's unique challenge lies in its process emissions, which account for over half of its CO2 output, independent of energy source. This means that simply decarbonizing the energy used in cement production is insufficient; innovative material solutions like Limestone Calcined Clay Cement (LC3) are needed to directly tackle these chemical process emissions.

Similarly, in steel production, the choice between coal-intensive blast furnaces and electric arc furnaces (which can use recycled steel and renewable electricity) profoundly impacts embodied carbon. This understanding underscores that sustainable building design must integrate material efficiency strategies, low-emission design, and the use of low-embodied carbon or carbon-storing materials, alongside electrification and renewable energy for operational needs. Policies promoting circularity, reuse, and bio-based materials are therefore as crucial as energy codes for new construction and retrofitting existing buildings to achieve a truly net-zero built environment. This comprehensive perspective ensures that efforts to reduce emissions are not merely shifting the carbon burden from one part of a building's lifecycle to another, but are instead driving systemic decarbonization 💬️.

concepts.title: bioenergy
concepts.body: Bioenergy is energy derived from organic materials, such as plants and animal waste, which can be converted into fuels or electricity.

concepts.title: energy storage
concepts.body: Energy storage refers to the capture and holding of energy for use at a later time, allowing for the balancing of supply and demand in energy systems.

concepts.title: hydrogen for development
concepts.body: Hydrogen for development refers to the use of hydrogen as a clean energy source to support economic growth, enhance energy security, and promote sustainable development, particularly in developing countries.

takeaways.title: Transport Emissions Demand Urgent Reduction Efforts.
takeaways.description: Transport accounts for over one-third of CO₂ emissions from end-use sectors, with emissions rising 3% in 2022 alone. To meet global climate goals, transport emissions must decline by over 3% annually until 2030, necessitating a shift toward cleaner energy sources, efficiency improvements, and policies promoting low-carbon mobility.

takeaways.title: Electrification is Key to Reducing Road Transport Emissions.
takeaways.description: Road transport is the largest contributor to transport emissions, making vehicle electrification a key solution. EV adoption is growing rapidly, with electric cars expected to make up nearly 50% of the global auto market by 2030. In developing countries, focusing on shared electric mobility, such as e-buses, two- and three-wheelers, can improve accessibility, cut costs, and support a just energy transition.

takeaways.title: Overcoming Key Challenges to Unlock Electrification’s Full Potential.
takeaways.description: Challenges such as high upfront costs, limited charging infrastructure, and increased demand for critical minerals must be addressed through targeted policies, innovative financing, and circular economy solutions like battery recycling. Ensuring local value addition in mineral-rich countries and preparing the workforce for new job opportunities are crucial to making transport electrification both sustainable and equitable.

content.title: Key Strategies and Solutions for Decarbonization

content.text:
4: Integrating clean cooking 💬️ and Renewable Energy

For policy makers in many developing countries, the building sector is the primary gateway for expanding energy access. Integrating clean cooking into national electrification plans, specifically through "eCooking" (electric cooking), can leverage investments in the power grid to solve the biomass crisis.

Simultaneously, "distributed renewable energy," such as rooftop solar PV, is transforming buildings from passive energy consumers into active producers. In Kenya, nearly 20% of homes now use solar power, and in India, city-wide rooftop solar models are helping to achieve both energy security and net-zero goals. These decentralized solutions can deliver modern energy services to rural and "hard-to-reach" areas more quickly and at a lower cost than traditional grid expansion.

3: Building Codes and Digital Transformation

Mandatory building energy codes are the foundation of a sustainable built environment. These codes set the minimum requirements for the "envelope" (walls, roof, windows) and the mechanical systems of a building. Today, only about 40% of new buildings constructed globally are covered by such codes, leaving a massive gap in rapidly growing economies.
To implement these codes effectively, governments must invest in "Quality Infrastructure." This includes establishing testing labs, like Vietnam’s Institute for Building Materials,and training a workforce in Building Performance Simulation (BPS). BPS allows designers to virtually "test" a building's energy performance under local climate conditions before it is built, optimizing features like shading and natural ventilation to meet the code requirements.

2: Regulatory Tools: MEPS and Labeling

While design and materials are critical, mandatory regulations are needed to shift the entire market. Minimum Energy Performance Standards (MEPS) and energy labeling are two of the most effective tools for improving the efficiency of appliances and equipment.
MEPS serve to "clean the market" by legally prohibiting the sale of the least efficient products. For policy makers, this is a powerful way to stop "environmental dumping", the practice of exporting inefficient appliances from developed countries to developing markets. Energy labels, on the other hand, use "comparative" or "endorsement" marks to inform consumers about the lifetime energy costs of a product, "nudging" them toward more efficient choices.

The Ghana Success Story: Faced with a massive influx of used, inefficient refrigerators from Europe, Ghana implemented a total ban on used cooling appliances and established strict MEPS and labeling for new ones. Supported by a "rebate scheme" that helped consumers buy new efficient models, the program reduced the average refrigerator's energy use from 1,200 kWh/year to 380 kWh/year. This project alone saved enough energy to equal 40% of the output of the national hydro dam and deferred $105 million in power generation investments.

Passive design is particularly valuable because it can be integrated into buildings at little to no extra cost if considered early in the design phase. It also makes a building more resilient to power outages, as the structure can maintain a liveable temperature even when the air conditioning is off.

1: Passive Design: The Power of Geometry and Climate

The most cost-effective strategy for decarbonization is "passive design." This involves designing a building to work with the local climate to maintain comfort without relying on mechanical heating or cooling.38 In the tropical and hot climates prevalent in many developing countries, passive design focuses primarily on "heat avoidance" and "natural cooling".

Orientation: Minimizing solar heat gain by facing the building correctly; for example, elongated designs with north–south facades reduce east–west sun exposure.
Shading: Using physical barriers to block direct sunlight; for example, overhangs, awnings, and traditional jaalis (perforated screens).
Natural Ventilation: Utilizing wind and air buoyancy to cool the interior; for example, cross-ventilation through well-placed windows and stack-effect vents.
Thermal Mass: Using dense materials to absorb and release heat slowly; for example, thick earth or brick walls that stay cool during the day and release heat at night.
Reflective Surfaces: Using light colors to bounce solar radiation away; for example, white roofs and light-colored walls to reduce the urban heat island effect.

To overcome these challenges, policy makers must adopt a holistic strategy that combines "Sufficiency, Efficiency, and Renewables" (the SER framework). This approach prioritizes avoiding demand first, then optimizing performance, and finally meeting the remaining energy needs with clean sources

Lack of standardized data and definitions

Finally, the lack of standardized data and definitions, often referred to as a "taxonomy", makes it difficult for financiers to identify what actually constitutes a "green" or "near-zero emission" building. This fragmentation leads to high transaction costs and investment uncertainty. Without clear, internationally recognized standards, the "green bond" or "green mortgage" markets cannot reach the scale necessary to transform the sector.

Zoning and building codes are frequently misaligned with the economic realities of low-income populations, leaving them with no choice but to build in hazardous or unregulated areas. For a policy maker, the challenge is to create standards that are "ambitious yet achievable," ensuring safety and efficiency without making housing unaffordable for the very people who need it most.

Split incentives
The "split incentive" problem is another major obstacle, particularly in urban rental markets. This occurs when the owner of the building pays for the energy-efficient upgrades, but the tenant pays the utility bills and thus reaps all the savings. Without a mechanism to share these benefits, neither party has a strong incentive to act. This is particularly problematic in residential decarbonization, where individual projects are often too small to attract large-scale private investors who prefer larger, more standardized projects like utility-scale wind or solar farms.

Capacity Gap
Capacity and expertise gaps also hinder progress. Many countries lack a workforce trained in modern green building techniques or the digital tools needed for "Building Performance Simulation" (BPS). In Vietnam, for instance, while there is a growing interest in energy-efficient buildings, the pool of architects and engineers proficient in advanced simulation software remains small. Furthermore, local government staff often lack the resources or training to effectively review and verify compliance with energy codes, leading to "paper codes" that are not enforced in the field.

Despite the clear benefits, the path to a decarbonized building sector is fraught with complex challenges. For policy makers in developing countries, these hurdles are often structural and deeply rooted in the local socio-economic context.

High upfront cost of sustainable technologies

While energy-efficient appliances or high-performance building materials offer long-term savings, they often require a higher initial investment than their "dirty" or inefficient counterparts. In many developing nations, widespread poverty and limited access to affordable credit mean that even a small price difference can make a sustainable option inaccessible to the average household. This is compounded by the "cost of capital" challenge. Clean energy and efficiency projects are often much more expensive to fund in developing countries than in advanced economies due to perceived risks, ranging from currency fluctuations to political instability. A solar farm or green housing project in South Africa may face significantly higher interest rates than a similar project in Germany, effectively penalizing the regions that most need the investment.

Informal construction
Another systemic hurdle is the "informal construction" sector. In many developing regions, particularly in Africa and South Asia, a significant portion of housing is constructed incrementally by families themselves, often without formal titles or compliance with building regulations. These buildings are "off the radar" for traditional policy tools.
This informality is often a response to the failure of formal land and housing systems to provide affordable options for the poor.

content.title: C: Key Challenges to the Industry Decarbonization

content.text:
Furthermore, buildings in developing countries are on the front lines of climate change impacts. They must not only be "low-carbon" but also "resilient." This means they must be able to withstand extreme heat, flooding, and storms. Retrofitting existing housing to be more resilient can save up to 68% of the embodied carbon compared to the emissions required to build new homes from scratch. In regions like the Caribbean or Southeast Asia, addressing the intersection of embodied carbon and housing resilience is both a mitigation strategy and an essential act of adaptation.
The socio-economic benefits of this transition are immense and extend far beyond environmental metrics. Energy efficiency is a "transformative, low-cost solution" that can fast-track access to affordable energy while boosting economic growth.
In countries like Türkiye and India, large-scale renovation and efficient appliance programs have already demonstrated these benefits. Türkiye’s renovation of public buildings saved enough energy to power 300,000 homes annually, while India’s efficient bulb program created thousands of direct and indirect jobs. For policy makers, these "multiple benefits" provide a compelling political and economic rationale for prioritizing the buildings sector in national climate plans (nationally determined contributions 💬️ or NDCs).

Another critical climate concept for the buildings sector is the "lock-in effect." Because buildings have long lifespans (often 50 years or more), the decisions made during the design and construction phase today will dictate energy consumption patterns well into the second half of the 21st century. If a new city district is built with poor insulation and inefficient cooling systems, retrofitting those buildings later will be significantly more expensive and difficult than building them correctly the first time. This is why the adoption of mandatory building energy codes is viewed as one of the most cost-effective climate actions available to governments.

The relationship between the building sector and climate change is profound and multi-dimensional. To meet the goals of the Paris Agreement and limit global warming to well below 2°C, the global buildings and construction sector must achieve near-complete decarbonization by 2050. This requires a paradigm shift in how policy makers view carbon emissions, moving beyond just "the light switch" to consider the "whole life cycle" of a building. This lifecycle approach categorizes emissions into two primary types: operational carbon and embodied carbon.

Operational carbon refers to the greenhouse gases emitted during the use of the building. These emissions result from the energy needed to heat, cool, light, and power a structure. Historically, building regulations have focused almost exclusively on this area, seeking to make air conditioners more efficient or improving wall insulation to keep heat out. In many developing countries, operational emissions are currently the dominant part of a building's footprint, particularly where the electricity grid is heavily dependent on coal or natural gas.
However, the "embodied carbon" of a building is increasingly recognized as an equally urgent challenge. This term refers to the emissions associated with the materials and construction processes throughout the whole lifecycle. It includes the carbon released during the extraction of raw materials, the manufacturing of products like cement and steel, transportation to the site, and the actual construction activity.In the context of rapid urbanization in the Global South, embodied carbon is a "sunk cost" that cannot be reversed. Once a massive concrete structure is built, its upfront carbon is already in the atmosphere.

content.title: B: Buildings, Energy, and Climate Change

content.text: The non-residential sector, encompassing offices, retail spaces, hospitals, and schools, accounts for the remaining 30% of the building sector's energy demand. While smaller in total volume than the residential sector, non-residential buildings often have higher energy intensity per square meter. They are also easier for policy makers to regulate through mandatory energy management systems and building codes, as seen in India’s Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC), which targets large commercial establishments with high connected loads.

A critical distinction in developing economies is the continued reliance on traditional biomass 💬️ for cooking. Approximately 2.1 billion people still lacked access to clean cooking fuels in 2022, relying instead on wood, charcoal, or agricultural waste. This reliance contributes to massive health, gender, and environmental costs, estimated at USD 2.4 trillion annually due to respiratory illnesses, the time burden on women for fuel collection, and localized deforestation. From a policy perspective, the transition to clean cooking, moving from open fires to electric induction or improved stoves is an essential component of the "buildings" energy conversation in the Global South.

Simultaneously, the demand for space cooling is surging. As global temperatures rise and urbanization intensifies, the "cooling gap" has become a major concern. Over one billion people currently lack access to sustainable cooling, which is vital for human comfort, health, and food security. Unlike the slow growth of heating demand in the North, the demand for air conditioning in EMDEs is expected to be a primary driver of electricity demand growth over the coming decades. In countries like Vietnam and Indonesia, where annual energy demand growth rates can reach 10%, managing this cooling load through efficient building design and appliance standards is essential for maintaining national energy security.
In the residential sector, which comprises roughly 70% of total building energy demand, the specific end-uses in developing countries reflect a unique set of challenges and opportunities.

Often described as a "sleeping giant" in climate policy, the built environment is a primary driver of global energy demand and greenhouse gas emissions. On a global scale, buildings and their associated construction processes account for approximately 32% of final energy consumption and are responsible for 34% of energy-related carbon dioxide emissions. When one accounts for the broader industrial activities required to produce construction materials such as cement, steel, and aluminum, the sector’s impact increases to nearly 37% or even 39% of global emissions. For policy makers, particularly those operating in developing nations, understanding how, where, and why energy is used in this sector is the first step toward crafting effective decarbonization strategies.

The way energy is consumed in buildings is not uniform; it varies significantly based on geography, economic status, and climate. In advanced economies, the building stock is largely mature, with energy demand driven by the maintenance and operation of existing structures. In these regions, space heating and water heating are the dominant end-uses, often accounting for 70% of residential energy consumption. However, the narrative for emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs) is drastically different. These regions are characterized by rapid urbanization, population growth, and rising middle-class incomes, which together create an unprecedented demand for new housing and commercial infrastructure. It is estimated that low- and middle-income countries in Africa and Asia will experience 93% of the world's urban population growth between 2020 and 2050. Consequently, the majority of the buildings that will exist in 2050 in these regions have not yet been built.

Sustainable Buildings: Efficiency, Electrification, and Equity

content.text: Lesson 2 Overview

The buildings sector, which includes construction, heating, cooling, lighting, and appliances, accounts for over one-third of global energy consumption and emissions. Operations alone are responsible for 30% of global final energy use and 26% of energy-related emissions, with 8% from direct emissions and 18% from indirect emissions tied to electricity and heat production.
While direct emissions slightly decreased to 3 Gt in 2022, indirect emissions rose to nearly 6.8 Gt due to increased reliance on electricity. Despite some progress, the sector remains off-track to meet the Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (NZE) Scenario. Addressing this requires a concerted effort to improve energy efficiency and adopt renewable energy technologies.
